content: Albizia lebbeck is a species of the genus Albizia, native to tropical regions of southern Asia. It has been extensively cultivated and has become naturalized in various tropical and subtropical areas around the world. Common English names for this tree include Lebbeck, Lebbeck Tree, Frywood, Siris, Koko, and Woman's-tongue-tree. This tree typically grows to a height of 18 to 30 meters, with a trunk diameter ranging from 50 centimeters to 1 meter. Its leaves are compound, measuring 5 to 15 centimeters in length, and consist of one to four pairs of pinnae, each pinna bearing 6 to 18 leaflets. The tree produces flowers with stamens that are approximately 8 centimeters long and are highly fragrant. Its seed pods are flat, broad, and contain six to twelve seeds. Uses Albizia lebbeck has a variety of uses, including applications in environmental management, forage, medicine, and timber production. It is commonly cultivated as a shade tree in regions of North and South America. In India, the tree is valued for its timber, while its bark is used medicinally to treat inflammation. Traditional Medicine In traditional medicine, Albizia lebbeck is employed for its astringent properties. It is used to treat boils, coughs, eye conditions, influenza, gingivitis, lung disorders, and pectoral issues. Additionally, it is used as a tonic and for the treatment of abdominal tumors. The tree is also known to have psychoactive properties. Its wood density is measured at 0.66 g/cm³ or higher.
